topic.title: Your quick-commerce price is yours alone
topic.claim: The discount on your quick-commerce app is not a gift, it is a bill the company pays to keep your habit alive.
topic.behaviour: You open the app for one item, find a cheap deal or a special store, and end up ordering twice a week. Two people in the same building may be shown different prices.
topic.mechanism: The app loses money on each order to make ordering from it automatic. Once you stop comparing, the discounts can shrink.
topic.group: Urban young professionals who order groceries on quick-commerce apps
topic.moment: You open the app for milk and leave with a snack, a face wash and a Rs 9 deal you did not plan for.

turn.believed: Cheap deals mean the app is being generous.
turn.actually: Discounts are a habit-building cost, and the price you see can depend on who the app thinks you are.

topic.feeling: managed, as if someone is steering the cart
topic.villain: a growth model that buys habits with discounts before it earns profit
topic.because: The app wants you back after you lapse. A low price for you and a normal price for someone else is cheaper than a blanket offer.

proof.fact: Discounts including brand-funded ones were 29% of Instamart's order value, up from 26% in June.
About 100 basis points of gross order value went into targeted investments, including a Rs 9 store and customer-group-specific pricing, to win back lapsed users.

topic.payoff: Test: open the app after a week away. If it is suddenly generous, it noticed you were gone.
topic.send_to: The friend who says they 'only order what's cheap' on the app.
real_details: Instamart's adjusted EBITDA loss widened to Rs 895 crore from Rs 778 crore
topic.news_peg: Swiggy September quarter results on Instamart discounts, reported 2026-10-26
topic.why_now: Results this month show the discount machine running harder, not softer.

sources.fact: Swiggy's Instamart discounts rose to 29% of order value from 26% in the June quarter. About 100 basis points of gross order value went into targeted investments, and contribution margin slipped back to -1% of gross order value.
sources.excerpt: discounts, including those funded by brands, accounted for 29% of Instamart's order value. [Discounts rose to 29% of order value from 26% in the June quarter.] About 100 basis points of gross order value went into what management calls targeted investments. [These include a Rs 9 store and prices tailored to particular customer groups.] Spending was aimed 'to win back lapsed users and build ordering habits.'

sources.fact: Swiggy blamed Instamart's 82 bps sequential fall in contribution margin to -1% of GOV partly on targeted pricing investments to reactivate dormant users. It also said Instamart's adjusted EBITDA losses peaked in Q2 FY27.
sources.excerpt: contribution margin deteriorated 82 basis points sequentially to -1% of GOV. [Swiggy linked this to 'targeted pricing investments' aimed at reactivating dormant users.] NOV, 'which excludes discounts from GOV,' rose 35% YoY and 13% QoQ to ₹6,594 Cr. Instamart's adjusted EBITDA margin 'improved marginally to -9.7% of GOV from -9.8%'. [Average monthly transacting users rose by 1.3 Mn sequentially to 14.8 Mn.]

cover.headline: That ₹9 Instamart deal is [a bill] Swiggy pays for your habit
cover.sub: The cheap price was never generosity. It has a job to do.

paragraphs:
That ₹9 deal on Instamart isn't a gift. It's Swiggy paying to keep your habit alive.
Swipe to read →
You open the app for milk. Your thumb adds chips and a face wash before you read a single price.
The ₹9 item goes in last, because it feels free. Your thumb taps it before you've decided anything. "Arre, nine rupees mein mil raha hai."
You meant to order once a week. It's now twice, often for one thing.
slides.why_swipe: Everyone does this. So what's actually going on?

paragraphs: We read cheap prices as the app being nice to us.
Swiggy has its own name for part of this spending: targeted investment. A discount is a cost the app chooses to pay, and kindness has nothing to do with it.
The deals feel bigger lately. They are.
In the September quarter, discounts were 29% of Instamart's order value, up from 26% in June. Brands fund part of it.
slides.why_swipe: Is everyone getting the same deal?

paragraphs: Swiggy says part of that spending goes to a ₹9 store and prices set for particular customer groups. The aim: win back lapsed users and build habits.
So you and your flatmate, on the same sofa, may be shown different prices.
slides.why_swipe: So are we just being played?

paragraphs: But the targeting serves the app. A sale for everyone costs a lot. A low price for people drifting away costs less, and wins them back.
Once you stop comparing with the shop downstairs, the offer can shrink.
slides.why_swipe: How can I tell if it's happening to me?

paragraphs: Stay off the app for a week, then open it.
If the deals suddenly look kinder, it isn't luck. The app got generous the week you stopped showing up.

end.save: Open this again the next time the app greets you with a ₹9 deal after a few quiet days.
end.send: Send to the friend who swears they only order what's cheap on the app, twice a week.
end.promise: How Indian brands really sell to you.

draft.caption: The cheapest thing in our cart is usually the one that brought us back.
draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text carousel from Above MRP arguing that discounts on Swiggy Instamart are a cost the company pays to build ordering habits. It shows typical habits: opening the app for milk and adding chips and a face wash without reading prices, tapping a ₹9 item last because it feels free, and ordering twice a week instead of once, often for one thing. It notes Swiggy calls part of this spending targeted investment, and that discounts, partly funded by brands, were 29% of Instamart's order value in the September quarter, up from 26% in June. Swiggy says part of its spending goes to a ₹9 store and prices for particular customer groups, to win back lapsed users and build habits, so flatmates may see different prices. It concedes ten-minute milk is useful, argues a low price for people drifting away costs the app less than a sale for everyone and can shrink once you stop comparing, and ends with a test: stay off the app for a week, and if the deals suddenly look kinder, the app got generous the week you stopped showing up.

claims.text: Swiggy describes part of its Instamart spending as targeted investments.
Discounts, including brand-funded ones, made up 29% of Instamart's order value in the September quarter, up from 26% in June.
Targeted investments included a ₹9 store and prices tailored to particular customer groups.
Swiggy said the targeted spending was meant to win back lapsed users and build ordering habits.
